source.title: Modeling Language as a Sequence of Thoughts

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It runs held-out loss sweeps over training-data size and parameter count, fits power laws, and compares the scaling behavior with a GPT-2 baseline, following the Kaplan-style measurement framework.
record.gate_note: The paper reports loss/perplexity scaling results and a father–son in-context direction-generalization probe. It also reports architecture-baseline comparisons at multiple training-token counts; those are included as loss-versus-data results. The ablation table and memory-gate analyses are not rows because they do not measure the claimed scaling relationships or downstream predictability.
record.test_reason: The paper fits Kaplan-style power laws to held-out loss over data (12M–50M tokens) and non-embedding parameters (0.34M–21.3M). It reports the curves for a standard GPT-2 baseline as well as its own architecture, in a new small-scale WikiText-103 setting. It also tracks a reversal-probe capability across the data-scaling checkpoints. It is not T1: the scale, corpus, early-stopped multi-epoch training and data range (under one order of magnitude) differ from the originals. It is not purely T4: the GPT-2 curves and exponents are reported results, and Table 2 losses fall at a near-constant log-log rate.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that TG is consistently more data- and parameter-efficient than matched GPT-2 at small scale, with the gain appearing as an intercept shift with similar exponents. Baseline comparisons show the gains depend on recurrence over semantically coherent sentence units. TG improves in-context reversal-direction generalization faster with data. They note the low-compute regime and say scaling up is needed.
record.recipe_differences: Uses held-out lexical-token test loss/perplexity and scaling sweeps over data and non-embedding parameter count, following the Kaplan-style framework. The models, corpus, scale, and experiments are different, and no compute-optimal allocation sweep is performed.
record.method_sensitivity: Architecture and recurrence design change observed perplexity: sentence-boundary markers help GPT-2, fixed token spans underperform sentence-based TG, and gist masking performs worse; within the reversal probe, the direction of the query and model scale affect the result.

fits_no_version.finding: A sentence-level recurrent architecture (TG) lowers loss at every data size and model size. Its fitted exponents are nearly identical to GPT-2's, so the gain is an intercept shift, equivalent to 1.05–1.08× data and 1.33–1.42× parameters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectural changes shift the intercept of loss scaling curves while leaving the exponent nearly unchanged.

record.problems: The scaling experiments are in a low-compute regime (up to 50M training tokens and approximately 85M non-embedding parameters) on WikiText-103. The parameter sweep varies width with depth fixed, and the study does not test compute-optimal allocation or large-scale extrapolation. The reversal-probe figures provide trends but the text does not give exact NLL values or uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: Ablation-table outcomes (Table 1) and memory-gate/gradient-share analyses (Appendices C–D) were omitted because they do not measure the claim versions' scaling laws or downstream predictability.

untested.parts: Compute scaling. Data range is only 12M–50M tokens (about 0.6 orders of magnitude), not several orders. No fit residuals are reported.
All: no prediction of runs orders of magnitude larger.
All: depth is held fixed while width varies; no shape comparison at fixed N.
Standard downstream benchmarks, and prediction of downstream performance from pretraining loss.
All: fitting choices are not varied.

missing.what: Fitted power-law exponents: data α≈0.149 (GPT-2) and 0.152 (TG); parameters α≈0.080 (GPT-2) and 0.081 (TG). Also the effective multipliers mD≈1.05–1.08 and mN≈1.33–1.42. No goodness-of-fit is given.

record.verdict_notes: Changed from T1 to T3: the setting is small-scale, multi-epoch, early-stopped WikiText-103 with a data range of under one order of magnitude. The power-law framework is used mainly to measure architecture efficiency, but the GPT-2 baseline curves bear on V1 in this narrow range. Recomputing from Table 2 gives GPT-2 local exponents of about 0.146–0.150 (data) and 0.077–0.087 (parameters), consistent with a power law. Removed the V1 limits_scope label on r17–r31: architecture differences in level do not qualify V1, and those rows have no fits. The V6 probe measures target-token NLL and margin, not a standard downstream benchmark, and r36/r37 are uncontrolled cross-model comparisons.

versions.untested_parts: Compute scaling is not swept; results cover training data and parameter count in a low-compute WikiText-103 setting.
The paper derives resource multipliers from fitted curves but does not test predictions from small runs against runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute-budget sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is measured.
The parameter sweep changes width while holding depth fixed; it does not compare depth, width, and other architectures at a fixed parameter count.
No other modalities or training regimes are tested.
The downstream-style result is limited to a father–son in-context direction-generalization probe; broader downstream tasks and prediction from pretraining loss are not tested.
The study does not systematically vary fitting choices or show that the fitted laws or compute-optimal allocations disagree or bend away from power laws.

rows.subject: Thought Gestalt (TG)
rows.size_stated: N ≈ 85M non-embedding parameters for the dataset-scaling checkpoints
rows.operation_detail: Father–son in-context completion probe; reports target-token NLL trend in the reversed query direction.
rows.value: target-NLL trend slope 0.263; lower target NLL at 30M and 50M; reverse-direction margin approximately −2.5 → −1.1 nats from 12M→50M
rows.note: The text says the target probability improves faster, but the reported margin remains negative through 50M, indicating a persisting distractor preference.
rows.check: For V6 the question is whether the probe improves with scale. TG's reversed-query target NLL improves (slope 0.263) and its margin improves monotonically (−2.5→−1.1 nats). A still-negative margin is not a failure to improve. Values are read partly from a figure.

rows.measure: target-token NLL trend and reverse-direction margin
rows.value: target-NLL trend slope 0.127; margin becomes more negative through 30M and only slightly recovers at 50M; distractor preference persists
rows.note: The text describes the trend and persistent reversal error but does not give exact margin values for GPT-2.

rows.subject: openai-community/gpt2-xl
rows.operation_detail: Father–son in-context completion probe comparing target and distractor preference.
rows.value: large in-context reversal error; distractor preferred over target
rows.note: The text explicitly describes the directional outcome; exact NLL values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: A single pretrained checkpoint with different data and training, so it is not a controlled scale step. It shows the reversal error persists at 1.5B.

rows.subject: Mistral 7B
rows.size_stated: 7 billion parameters; trained on trillions of tokens
rows.operation_detail: Father–son in-context completion probe comparing target and distractor preference.
rows.note: The text says the in-context directional bias is largely absent at 7B scale; exact NLL values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: A single pretrained checkpoint with a different architecture and data. It shows the error resolved at 7B, so scale is confounded with training differences.

relationships.condition: GPT-2 and TG, 85M non-embedding params, 12M–50M WikiText-103 tokens; and 0.34M–21.3M params at 50M tokens (width varied, depth 12)
relationships.reason: Test loss falls at a near-constant log-log rate. Reported exponents are data α≈0.149/0.152 and parameters α≈0.080/0.081. This holds only over a narrow, small-scale range (r1–r16).
relationships.display_finding: Test loss decreased at nearly constant logarithmic rates, with data exponents of approximately 0.149/0.152 and parameter exponents of 0.080/0.081 over narrow ranges.

relationships.condition: TG reversed query, and both models on the normal query, across the 12M–50M data-scaling checkpoints
relationships.reason: Target NLL improves with data: slopes 0.263 (TG reversed), 0.347 (TG normal) and 0.357 (GPT-2 normal). TG's margin improves monotonically (r32, r34, r35).
relationships.display_finding: Target negative log-likelihood improved with slopes of 0.263 for TG reversed queries, 0.347 for TG normal queries and 0.357 for GPT-2 normal queries, while TG’s margin increased at every data step.

relationships.condition: Standard transformers on the reversed in-context father–son query
relationships.reason: GPT-2's margin worsens through 30M tokens and barely recovers at 50M. The error persists in GPT-2 XL (1.5B) and is gone only in Mistral 7B, so improvement is non-monotone and architecture-dependent (r33, r36, r37).
relationships.display_finding: GPT-2's margin worsened through 30M tokens and barely recovered at 50M; the error persisted in GPT-2 XL at 1.5B but disappeared in Mistral 7B.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: TG and GPT-2 dataset-size sweeps on WikiText-103, 12M–50M training tokens; parameter-size sweeps at 50M tokens
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports power-law fits to held-out test loss, with similar exponents for TG and GPT-2 (dataset: TG α ≈ 0.152, GPT-2 α ≈ 0.149; parameters: TG α ≈ 0.081, GPT-2 α ≈ 0.080), and test perplexity falls across the reported sweeps (r1–r16). The tested ranges are limited.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Alternative architecture baselines across 20M–50M training tokens
reader_labels.reason: Sentence-boundary and fixed-span variants have higher perplexity than TG at some or all reported scales, while gist masking is substantially worse than both GPT-2 and TG; these comparisons are not themselves reported as power-law fits (r17–r31).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: TG and GPT-2 on the normal and reversed father–son in-context probe
reader_labels.reason: The target-NLL trends improve with training data; TG improves faster than GPT-2 in the reversed condition, while their normal-condition slopes are nearly equal (r32–r35).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Reversed father–son query at the tested scales and models
reader_labels.reason: TG's reverse-direction margin remains negative through 50M, GPT-2 retains a distractor preference, and GPT-2 XL shows a large reversal error; the probe reports that Mistral 7B prefers the target in both directions (r32, r33, r36, r37).
